prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with topological insulators first and the lattice clock fourth, and after the first round I move the clock to the top of my configuration. The reason is the one I would normally apply to my own candidate: what is the simple, general mechanism and who identified it? For the lattice clock the answer is exact and attributable. Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels the differential light shift so that a trapping lattice does not perturb the clock transition, while Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil shifts and thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. That is a clean idea, analysable from first principles, and it has been checked against experiment in many laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) at the 1e-18 level, with millimetre-scale redshift tests and bounds on varying constants following from it. Two names, Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for the accuracy and many-body programme, carry it, and no other member disputes the pair. My own candidate cannot meet that standard under a three-person limit. The mature, well-confirmed physics of the quantum spin Hall effect is not in doubt, but the credit problem was sharpened rather than resolved in round one.
statement.case_against: The reservation I raised in round one has not vanished: this is a third prize in the precision-metrology line after the 2005 comb prize (Ye is a repeat laureate) and the 2012 ion-clock prize, and a sceptic can say the new physics is partly engineering towards 1e-18. The Sr-lattice priority history among Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST has also not been verified from the record, and I cannot judge it myself. Finally, if the committee prefers the discovery of a phenomenon to an instrument, B013 remains the stronger fit for that criterion, and I regret that its attribution (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the names; Mele versus Hasan) makes it unprepared this year.

responses.point: Kroll argues that waiting for the SI redefinition would risk honouring a roadmap step instead of the discovery, since the clocks' performance is already established and independently confirmed.
responses.response: I accept this and withdraw the timing objection. The redefinition is a metrological decision that will follow from the evidence, so it neither adds to nor subtracts from the physics that a citation would describe. My remaining question is the narrower one about novelty, and your point that many-atom interrogation in a lattice free of first-order shifts is not covered by the 2005 or 2012 citations answers it well enough. I also note your disclosure of the year in Hall's laboratory. It is a lineage tie rather than a collaboration, and I do not think it affects the pair of names, which every member has proposed independently.

responses.point: Johansson accepts that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are an excellent set but says the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal leaves an awkward attribution hole and that he would cite the quantum spin Hall effect alone rather than cover Hasan's strand.
responses.response: We agree on the content and it moves me. I defended the triple in round one on the ground that Z2 time-reversal-symmetric topology differs from the 2016 theme, and I still hold that. But the BHZ omission cannot be repaired within three names, and a prize that has to be explained with an apology in its citation is weaker than one where credit maps directly onto concept and demonstration. I would keep B013 as my alternative and would revisit it in a cycle where a defensible trio exists, perhaps with the experimental side of the 3D strand settled.

responses.point: Danielsson presses what has been learned about nature from the lattice clocks given that the fundamental-physics tests so far are null results, and he lists the Higgs discovery as his first choice.
responses.response: A null result at 1e-18 is still a statement about nature, a bound on drifts of constants and on couplings to ultralight dark matter, and the millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a positive test of general relativity in a laboratory. But I agree the prize should rest on the new physical regime that was opened and demonstrated and not on promised discoveries, which is why the citation I propose names the magic-wavelength trapping and the 10^-18 level. On the Higgs, I share your view of its importance. My difficulty is the same as the one you state yourself: four names for three places, and two collaborations of thousands, so any trio is contestable in a way the clock pair is not.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration-corrected microscopy as a statutory invention and flags thin opening support and the uncredited STEM corrector work of Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini.
responses.response: I take the point about the word invention and withdraw any suggestion that instrument prizes are less eligible: the lattice clock is itself an instrument-level advance and I should be consistent. What separates the two for me is the open priority question you flag, which an expert report may or may not settle, whereas the clock pair is uncontested. If the reports show that the TEM and STEM correctors can be separated cleanly, I would regard B052 as a respectable candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B053 from twisted bilayer graphene and shares my maturity concern on B033 while saying B013 is strained on attribution but would be acceptable with an imperfect split.
responses.response: We have converged on the same ordering for similar reasons. I agree that B033 should wait: the pairing mechanism is unresolved, Cao is outside the credited names, and a mechanism that is not understood is a poor basis for a citation. On B013, I continue to disagree about dropping Mele, since the Z2 classification is the joint Kane-Mele idea, but I accept your point that an imperfect split is a cost the committee need not bear this year when a cleaner candidate is available.

uncertainties: Whether expert reports confirm that Katori and Ye are the right and sufficient pair given the Sr-lattice priority history, including Lemonde, Ludlow, Hall and Peik.
Whether the committee regards Ye as a repeat laureate for a distinct step or as a third prize in one metrology line.
Whether a defensible triple for B013 can ever be agreed given the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the separate 3D strand, which affects whether I would return to it.
How much weight to give the 2016 topology prize in judging novelty for B013.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict. My co-authors work on turbulence, aerosols and complex systems and none of the credited candidates for B053 or my alternatives are among them. My Gothenburg ties with Johansson and Olsson are institutional only. I have no connection to Hall's or Katori's groups.
